We disagree on exercise. Walking is best, practically a must. Then heavy compound lifts, even for women and older people. Then low impact, low skill, high intensity interval training. This means it's less likely to injure you. Exercises include: stationary bike, rowing machine, prowler pushes. Swimming is also great, but higher skill. Running also okay, but higher impact and greater chance of injury. Boxing/wrestling/mma is high impact, high skill, relatively high risk of injury, but good training and fun. First warm up for a couple of minutes, then 4 to 8 intervals of 10 to 60 seconds work (I usually do 25 seconds) with about 3 times the work time in "active" rest (so 75 seconds for ne), e.g. keep walking.

This is good advice; the exercises you listed are all excellent. However, I think you're underestimating running. Humans were designed for running. Besides our intelligence, it is our ability to run for extended periods of time that set us apart in the animal kingdom. It is so core to our evolution that it is a necessary exercise. Athletes of all kinds run. Athletes who don't apply running technique to their sport (e.g. boxers) run. Done with good form and on good terrain, combined with a healthy diet high enough in the nutrients needed to maintain the bones/ligaments/etc., running is the best form of cardio there is.

The reason I recommend bicycling and running is that you can do it to and from work (or wherever you go). Which means you don't have to spend time in the gym, which is something that is required of lifting, prowlers, swimming, and combat sports. The stationary bike is less efficient than actual bicycling (same as a treadmill; less fun, less gain), so it doesn't make any sense to me to use that when bicycling and running are alternatives. As for the rowing machine, many small gyms don't have them.

Essentially, running and bicycling are the best introductory exercises for someone who doesn't exercise at all.
